title: The Ethics of Advanced AI Assistants

bias_targets.methodology: Theoretical analysis and literature review of sociotechnical harms and access disparities, citing previous empirical studies on facial recognition algorithms and automated speech recognition systems (e.g., African American Vernacular English).

Literature review and conceptual analysis of anthropomorphic design choices (e.g., default female-sounding voice assistants) and how they inadvertently reinforce gendered stereotypes and societal role associations.

Theoretical discussion of quality-of-service disparities based on existing empirical literature, highlighting performance degradation in AI assistants when processing non-English languages, regional dialects, and specific accents.

Conceptual analysis of how hyper-personalized AI assistants might align with user expectations to produce ideologically biased statements, reinforcing filter bubbles, confirmation bias, and political polarization.
Theoretical analysis of digital inequality and systemic access restrictions resulting from physical infrastructure gaps, digital literacy levels, and financial barriers like prohibitive paywalls.
Literature review of accessibility challenges, proposing a 'design for the margins' and liberatory access framework to prevent algorithmic exclusion and better accommodate differently abled users.
